rationale: PixiJS gives a small WebGL-based 2D runtime with sprite batching, blend modes, containers, and custom shader filters, which is well suited to the PoC's neon additive particles, bloom, screen shake, and chromatic aberration. It is lighter and more 2D-focused than Three.js or PlayCanvas, more visually flexible than raw Canvas 2D, and leaner for this single-screen juice loop than a full Phaser setup. Framework-free WebGL would give maximum control but adds avoidable scene-graph, batching, and filter plumbing cost for a PoC. Main tradeoff: custom hit-stop, chromatic aberration, and bloom likely need small custom Pixi shader or container logic, and Pixi adds bundle weight versus a hand-written renderer.
setup: Use npm/Vite: create a vanilla TypeScript project with npm create vite@latest prism-breaker -- --template vanilla-ts; install pixi.js and tone with npm install pixi.js tone. Build a fixed 1280x720 PixiJS WebGL scene containing one paddle, one ball, one wall area, and one row of bricks; implement circle-vs-rectangle collision, mouse/keyboard paddle control, and click/space ball launch. Add a root container for screen shake, simple hit-stop via scaled delta time, additive particle bursts, combo-tier intensity, and a small custom PixiJS filter for bloom and chromatic aberration. Use Tone.js synths for a color-note map, brick-hit chiptune notes, a simple main loop, and a game-over sting, with score, lives, mute, and restart. Verify in latest Chromium with npm run dev: launch the ball, clear the bricks, observe distinct escalating combo juice, hear brick notes aligned with destruction bursts without drift, restart cleanly, and confirm no console errors.
